# BTRFS: The Spice of Efficient CI Cycles with Docker

At Devoxx France 2018, Nicolas Muller and Cédric Vandome delivered a talk titled *BTRFS, l’épice des bons cycles de CI avec Docker*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGY8ERuL0YI). They explored BTRFS, a Linux filesystem, and its synergy with Docker to streamline continuous integration (CI) for massive datasets. Addressing a real-world challenge—managing a 500GB database on a single 1TB disk for multiple developers—they demonstrated how BTRFS’s copy-on-write snapshots enable fast, space-efficient CI cycles. This session is a gem for DevOps engineers and developers optimizing CI pipelines with large data volumes.

## The Problem: CI with Massive Databases

Muller and Vandome framed their talk around a common pain point: running CI with a 500GB database in feature-branch workflows. Developers frequently corrupt the database, requiring time-consuming restores that disrupt testing. With limited storage (a single 1TB disk) and no budget for additional drives, traditional solutions like duplicating data for each developer are impractical. The speakers shared their experience at a client site, where slow provisioning and storage constraints crippled productivity, setting the stage for BTRFS as a lightweight, efficient solution.

## Why BTRFS? A Filesystem for Snapshots

BTRFS, introduced in 2008, is a copy-on-write filesystem that creates instant, space-efficient snapshots at the block level, unlike file-level systems like AUFS. Muller explained its stability, with community support despite Red Hat’s 2017 withdrawal, and its integration into Linux distributions like SUSE. By formatting a disk with BTRFS, developers can create subvolumes and snapshots without duplicating data, making it ideal for CI environments. The speakers highlighted BTRFS’s low overhead compared to LVM, which struggles with complex delta-based snapshots, offering a developer-friendly alternative.

## BTRFS and Docker in Action

The duo demonstrated BTRFS in a CI pipeline using Jenkins and Docker. They mounted a BTRFS-formatted disk into a Jenkins container, installing BTRFS tools to manage snapshots. For each Git commit, a Jenkinsfile dynamically creates a Docker Compose file, provisioning a Java application and a PostgreSQL database. BTRFS snapshots provide each branch with an isolated 500GB dataset, created instantly without duplicating storage. A demo showed a master branch snapshot occupying only 107MB, despite appearing as 106MB per branch, thanks to BTRFS’s pointer-based deduplication. This setup enabled developers to test rapidly without manual restores.

## Advanced Use Cases and Cautions

Beyond CI, Muller and Vandome explored BTRFS’s integration with Docker’s storage drivers, allowing containers to leverage BTRFS snapshots natively. They introduced a Docker volume plugin for simplified snapshot management, reducing the need for privileged containers. However, they cautioned against using BTRFS with complex RAID setups (e.g., RAID 5/6) in production due to potential data corruption risks. For development and testing, BTRFS shines, but production use requires careful configuration. The speakers also showcased Testcontainers, a library that uses BTRFS snapshots for integration testing, enabling developers to run real databases without mocking.

# Web Components: Rainbows and Unicorns?

In a concise talk at Devoxx France 2018, Sarah Harkousse, a front-end developer at Dassault Systèmes, explored *Web Components: It’s all rainbows and unicorns! Is it?*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R-Dn5A5toX8). Harkousse demystified web components, a set of W3C standards promising modular, reusable HTML elements. While exciting, their adoption faces hurdles like performance issues and partial browser support. This pragmatic session offers developers a clear starting point for using ES6 web components in production.

## Web Components: The Basics

Web components leverage four standards: HTML templates, shadow DOM, custom elements, and HTML imports. Harkousse demonstrated creating a custom button using the `<template>` tag for inert markup, shadow DOM for CSS encapsulation, and custom elements for programmable tags. Despite their simplicity, she noted that templates aren’t revolutionary, and HTML imports face deprecation risks due to performance concerns and the rise of ES modules.

## Browser Support and Practical Tips

Harkousse addressed web components’ Achilles’ heel: inconsistent browser support. Google’s Polymer team provides polyfills like `webcomponents.js`, but these introduce performance overhead and behavioral differences. She advised using shadow DOM only when natively supported and favoring ES modules over HTML imports. For custom elements, Harkousse recommended extending native elements (e.g., `HTMLButtonElement`) to inherit built-in behaviors, ensuring robust, future-proof components.

# Hexagonal Architecture for Beginners

At Devoxx France 2018, Yannick Chéne, a Java developer and CTO at SFEIR, presented a talk titled *Architecture hexagonale pour les nuls*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Hi5aDfRe-aE). Aimed at Spring developers, Chéne introduced hexagonal architecture (also known as ports and adapters) to manage software complexity using Domain-Driven Design (DDD) principles. Through Kotlin code examples, he bridged DDD’s theoretical focus with practical Spring integration, making it accessible for Java developers.

## The Case for Hexagonal Architecture

Yannick shared a real-world issue: a Spring-like application with slow, complex logic scattered across layers, making maintenance a nightmare. Traditional layered architectures often mix business rules with infrastructure, leading to code like nested `if` statements in DAOs. Hexagonal architecture isolates the domain (business logic) from infrastructure, using ports (interfaces) and adapters (implementations) to manage interactions, ensuring cleaner, testable code.

## Building a Domain-Centric Application

Using a feature-voting platform as an example, Yannick demonstrated a domain model in Kotlin with entities like `Feature` and `Vote`, free of framework dependencies. Business rules, such as vote score calculations, reside in the domain. Primary ports (services) expose domain functionality to the outside, while secondary ports (interfaces) handle external interactions like database access. Adapters, implemented with Spring, connect these ports to REST controllers and MongoDB, maintaining domain purity.

## Spring Integration and Benefits

Yannick showed how Spring’s dependency injection wires adapters to ports, keeping the domain framework-agnostic. A REST controller calls a domain service, which uses a MongoDB adapter to persist data. This separation simplifies testing, speeds up development, and enhances scalability by centralizing business logic. However, Chéne noted challenges, like managing DTO mappings, and emphasized the need for team training to adopt this approach effectively.

# Spectre and Meltdown: 15 Minutes to Understand

At Devoxx France 2018, Alexis Duque, an R&D engineer at Ertz Hommes, delivered a quickie titled *Spectre et Meltdown, 15 min pour tout comprendre*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fsV4R5Fvn2g). Duque unpacked the Spectre and Meltdown vulnerabilities, major CPU flaws discovered in early 2018, explaining their mechanics, origins, and countermeasures. This session offers developers a concise primer on side-channel attacks and their impact on modern processors.

## How Spectre and Meltdown Work

Duque explained that Spectre and Meltdown exploit CPU optimizations like out-of-order execution and branch prediction. Meltdown allows unauthorized access to kernel memory by bypassing access checks, leveraging timing attacks on memory cache to read sensitive data. Spectre manipulates branch prediction to trick processors into executing malicious code paths, accessing restricted memory. Both rely on side-channel attacks, measuring memory access times to infer data, a technique pioneered by researchers globally, including Google’s Project Zero and Graz University.

## Impacts and Fixes

These vulnerabilities affect nearly all modern CPUs, enabling attackers to steal private data or alter application behavior. Duque highlighted fixes like KAISER (Kernel Address Isolation), which isolates kernel memory to mitigate Meltdown, with minimal performance impact on newer processors. Spectre, however, requires complex microcode updates and software patches, with partial fixes for its variants. Developers can check system vulnerability using tools on Windows and Unix systems, though new side-channel attacks continue to emerge.

# Mutation Testing: Ensuring Test Quality

In a quickie at Devoxx France 2018, Sahraoui Buisson, a Java expert at Xenia, presented *Mutation Testing comment vous assurer de la qualité de vos tests*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mNrZYw0nU1k). Buisson introduced mutation testing with Pitest to evaluate unit test effectiveness, revealing gaps in code coverage. This session is essential for developers aiming to validate the robustness of their test suites.

## Why Mutation Testing?

Buisson emphasized that a good test fails when code behaves unexpectedly, not just when it runs. Traditional code coverage metrics, even at 100%, don’t guarantee quality, as tests may execute code without verifying behavior. Mutation testing introduces deliberate changes (mutations) like altering operators or conditions, checking if tests detect these “bugs.” If tests pass despite mutations, the code lacks sufficient coverage, highlighting weak tests.

## Using Pitest

Buisson demonstrated Pitest, a Java plugin integrated via Maven or Gradle, which generates mutated code copies and runs tests against them. A demo on a FizzBuzz kata showed Pitest’s reports, marking lines green if mutations are caught and red if tests miss them. While effective, mutation testing can be slow, taking hours on large projects, but scoping to critical logic improves performance. It’s a powerful tool to ensure tests catch real errors, especially in TDD-driven projects.

# Reconcile with JavaScript Using Flow

Thuy Nguyen, a full-stack JS developer at Fluo, presented a quickie at Devoxx France 2018 titled *Réconciliez-vous avec le JS grâce à Flow*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ua3MaGkPv80). Nguyen introduced Flow, a static type checker from Facebook, to write robust, maintainable JavaScript. This session is ideal for developers seeking to tame JavaScript’s dynamic typing.

## Why Flow?

JavaScript’s weak, dynamic typing leads to runtime errors, like null multiplications or late-detected bugs. Nguyen explained that Flow, used extensively at Fluo and Facebook, catches these issues pre-execution via static type inference. Installed via npm and integrated with tools like VS Code, Flow incrementally types code with annotations, ensuring compatibility with existing projects.

## Best Practices

Nguyen demonstrated Flow catching errors in examples, such as invalid function arguments. She shared practices: avoid overly permissive types (e.g., nullable strings), use union types for state machines to prevent invalid states, and leverage read-only arrays to avoid mutation issues. These ensure maintainable code, making Flow a powerful ally for large-scale JavaScript projects.

# Let’s Sketchnote: Visual Note-Taking

At Devoxx France 2018, Amélie Diaz de Tuesta and Aurore Benoit, developers at Lectra, delivered a quickie titled *Let’s Sketchnote prise de notes visuelle*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sxyHF5pptgY). They introduced sketchnoting, a creative method to capture notes visually using simple drawings, text, and symbols. This session equips developers with a fun, accessible tool to enhance communication and retention.

## Why Sketchnote?

Sketchnoting combines text and visuals like pictograms, arrows, and containers to make notes engaging and memorable. The speakers emphasized its universal appeal, as visuals transcend language barriers, though cultural differences may affect interpretation. It aids comprehension by simplifying complex ideas, boosts concentration during meetings, and enhances memorization, as studies show drawings are recalled better than text. Sketchnoting also fosters creativity, balancing the analytical mindset common among developers.

## How to Sketchnote

Anyone with basic drawing skills can sketchnote. Start with simple shapes—circles, squares, triangles—to create pictograms like stick figures or symbols for concepts like solutions (lightbulbs) or risks (warning signs). Use uppercase text, selective bolding, and two to three colors for clarity. Structures like linear layouts or mind maps organize ideas, while arrows and containers link concepts. Shadows add polish but prioritize content over aesthetics. Sketchnotes can be created live during conferences or redrawn from traditional notes, improving with practice.

# Literate Programming: The Story of Your Code

R. Lemaire presented a quickie at Devoxx France 2018 titled *Litterate programming le roman de votre programme*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Et-19gh2C5A). Lemaire revived Donald Knuth’s 1984 concept of literate programming, blending code with natural language to create executable programs and readable essays. This session explores its relevance for modern developers.

## What Is Literate Programming?

Introduced by Knuth, literate programming treats code as an essay, interleaving natural language explanations with executable code snippets via macros. The source generates both a program and a printable document, prioritizing human understanding over machine execution. Unlike traditional comments, it follows the programmer’s thought process, not the program’s structure, using tools like WEB to weave code and text. Lemaire highlighted its artistic appeal, merging technical and creative expression.

## Benefits and Challenges

Literate programming forces developers to deeply understand their code, as explaining it in natural language reveals gaps in logic. It produces clear, self-documenting programs, ideal for complex systems. However, it demands proficiency in both coding and writing, which can be daunting. Maintaining such programs is challenging, as refactoring text-heavy code is less straightforward than modern practices like unit testing. Lemaire’s experiment adapting it to Java showed its verbosity but suggested writing natural language explanations before coding to capture its benefits.

# Best Practices for Java in Docker

At Devoxx France 2018, Charles Sabourdin, a freelance architect, and Jean-Christophe Sirot, an engineer at Docker, delivered a session titled *Java dans Docker Bonnes pratiques*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vzpU2jxrxJ8). They explored common pitfalls when running Java applications in Docker containers, focusing on memory management issues that cause crashes or performance degradation in production. This session offers practical solutions for developers and ops teams.

## Memory Management Challenges

Java applications in Docker often behave unpredictably due to mismatched memory settings. The speakers introduced a sample app, ResourceMunger, which intentionally consumes excessive memory, triggering crashes like OutOfMemoryError. A key issue is Docker’s `--memory` flag (e.g., `-m 512m`), which limits container memory, but Java’s JVM (pre-Java 9) ignores these limits, assuming access to the host’s total RAM. This leads to over-allocation, where the JVM’s heap (set via `-Xmx`) exceeds Docker’s constraints, causing the operating system to kill the container or resort to slow swap memory, degrading performance.

## Solutions and Best Practices

To align JVM memory with Docker limits, use Java 8 update 131+ or Java 9+ with experimental flags like `-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions` and `-XX:+UseCGroupMemoryLimitForHeap`. These enable the JVM to respect container memory constraints, automatically setting the heap to a fraction (e.g., 1/4) of the allocated memory. In Java 10, this behavior is default, eliminating the need for `-Xmx` flags, though specifying them can revert to legacy behavior. Disabling swap (`--memory-swappiness=0`) prevents performance issues, ensuring crashes are fast and diagnosable. Tools like `show-settings` and profilers help monitor memory usage, while build plugins (e.g., Maven’s Fabric8) streamline Docker integration.

# HashiCorp Nomad: Lean Microservices in Production

Jérôme Devoucoux, a developer at Jin, presented a session at Devoxx France 2018 titled *HashiCorp Nomad: Une architecture microservices lean en Prod*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mTzabg-U09M). He detailed Jin’s transition from Kubernetes to HashiCorp’s Nomad for orchestrating a microservices-based monitoring tool, Player, on AWS. This session highlights Nomad’s simplicity and scalability for production environments.

## Nomad’s Role in Microservices

Player, Jin’s SaaS tool, tracks online reputations by processing real-time data streams, handling 1,000 entries per second with 100ms API response times. Initially, Jin used manual server management, which was maintenance-heavy. Nomad, paired with Consul, Vault, and Terraform, enabled a lean microservices architecture. Nomad’s master-worker model dynamically scales containers, isolating resources and adapting to fluctuating loads. Consul provides service discovery, Vault secures secrets, and Terraform automates infrastructure. The cluster, built on AWS, ensures high availability with multi-master setups and persistent storage via Elasticsearch and S3.

## Production Stability and Monitoring

To ensure production readiness, Jin stress-tested the cluster in pre-prod using chaos engineering, simulating master failures and worker crashes. Key lessons included configuring Nomad’s restart policies to handle failed container deployments, tuning garbage collection to prevent network saturation, and reserving CPU for critical tasks. Prometheus and Grafana monitored CPU, RAM, disk, and Nomad-specific metrics (e.g., allocation counts), with alerts set at thresholds like 75% disk usage. These practices stabilized the system, supporting 13,200 containers and 42 million documents across 50 projects.

# Improving Code Quality with Cognitive Complexity

Xavier Bourguignon from SonarSource delivered a quickie at Devoxx France 2018 titled *Améliorer la qualité du code source à l’aide de la Complexité Cognitive*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=I1TsKxW-sS8). He introduced cognitive complexity, a modern metric surpassing cyclomatic complexity for assessing code maintainability. This session equips developers with tools to write clearer, more maintainable code.

## Understanding Cognitive Complexity

Cyclomatic complexity, a 1970s metric, counts execution paths but overlooks modern code nuances, often equating simple switches with nested loops. Cognitive complexity, introduced by SonarSource in 2016, measures mental effort required to understand code, ignoring clear structures (e.g., method declarations) and penalizing nested constructs like ifs, loops, or ternaries. For example, a nested loop with an if scores higher (e.g., 7) than a flat switch (e.g., 1), reflecting true comprehension difficulty. SonarCloud analysis of Hadoop revealed high-scoring classes (e.g., BlockManager at 853), pinpointing maintenance hotspots.

## Refactoring for Clarity

To reduce cognitive complexity, Bourguignon recommends techniques from *Clean Code*: collapse nested ifs, use early returns, replace chained conditionals with switches, and leverage multi-catch for exceptions. Classpath libraries simplify repetitive patterns, and small, well-named methods enhance readability. SonarQube (version 6.6+) flags methods exceeding a complexity threshold (default: 15), guiding refactoring. These practices, applied to open-source projects, demonstrably improve code quality, making it easier for teams to maintain and extend.

# Applications Web with Spring Boot 2.0

In a captivating presentation at DevoxxFR2018, Stéphane Nicoll unveiled the transformative capabilities of Spring Boot 2.0, specifically highlighting its profound impact on the landscape of web application development. The session delved into how this iteration of Spring Boot empowers developers to construct reactive applications using Spring WebFlux, all while preserving the comprehensive functionalities that have become synonymous with the Spring ecosystem. Nicoll's insights emphasized the shift towards a more resilient and scalable architecture, crucial for modern web services.

## The Reactive Paradigm with Spring WebFlux

At the core of Spring Boot 2.0's advancements lies the embrace of reactive programming, a paradigm designed to handle asynchronous data streams efficiently and non-blockingly. Stéphane illuminated how Spring WebFlux, built upon Project Reactor, offers a compelling alternative or complement to the traditional Spring MVC approach. This new framework provides a fresh perspective on crafting web applications, particularly well-suited for scenarios demanding high concurrency and low latency. It allows developers to manage interactions with slow clients or overloaded external services with grace, ensuring a fluid user experience even under challenging network conditions. Rather than forcing a complete overhaul, Spring Boot 2.0 presents WebFlux as an additional choice, enabling development teams to selectively adopt reactive patterns where they yield the most significant benefits, ensuring that existing Spring MVC applications remain fully supported and viable. The flexibility to choose between these two powerful models underscores Spring's commitment to adaptability and performance.

## Enhancements and Practical Applications

Stéphane Nicoll meticulously detailed the myriad improvements and novel features integrated into Spring Boot 2.0 that extend beyond the reactive model. The presentation showcased how tools like Actuator and Developer Tools are refined to provide unparalleled operational insights and development efficiency. Actuator, for instance, offers robust endpoints for monitoring, managing, and inspecting applications in production, while Developer Tools streamlines the development cycle with features like automatic restarts and live reloads, significantly boosting productivity. Furthermore, Spring Boot 2.0 strengthens its support for crucial components such as Spring Data and Spring Security, ensuring that reactive applications can seamlessly integrate with data persistence layers and robust security mechanisms. Through compelling live coding examples, Stéphane demonstrated practical use cases where the reactive architecture excels. These included managing data streams from numerous IoT devices, efficiently handling sluggish client connections that might otherwise impede server performance, and gracefully interacting with remote services that could be prone to delays or failures. The inherent design of reactive programming, facilitated by WebFlux, allows applications to remain responsive and resource-efficient, making it an ideal choice for complex, distributed systems.

## Evolution and Future Directions

Spring Boot 2.0 marks a significant evolutionary step, fundamentally built on Java 8, which provides the bedrock for many of its contemporary features, including functional programming constructs. Stéphane underscored that this release is not merely an incremental update but a pivotal advancement that reflects the continuous innovation within the Spring ecosystem. The introduction of `WebFlux.fn` further exemplifies this forward-thinking approach, offering a functional programming model for defining web endpoints that can lead to more concise and testable code. The framework’s commitment to providing an adaptive environment means that while the core Spring Framework 5 forms the foundation, Spring Boot 2.0 makes it remarkably easy to harness these advanced capabilities with minimal configuration. This ease of use is a hallmark of Spring Boot, abstracting away much of the boilerplate, allowing developers to concentrate on business logic. The ongoing development efforts ensure that Spring Boot remains at the forefront of enterprise Java, continuously adapting to new architectural patterns and technological shifts, empowering developers to build sophisticated and performant applications for the challenges of tomorrow.

# A Father and Son's Code Odyssey: "Un Loof ça va, de Loof bonjour les dégâts"

In a heartwarming and often humorous session at DevoxxFR2018, Nicolas De Loof, accompanied by his son Thomas De Loof, shared a deeply personal narrative about the transmission of a passion for coding across generations. This unique father-and-son duo presented a candid exploration of how the digital world can bridge generational gaps, recounting the unexpected twists and turns when a seasoned developer attempts to impart his love for programming to his child. Their story wasn't just about code; it was a testament to the evolving nature of learning, the surprises of rediscovery, and the power of play in education.

## Rekindling the Spark: From Retro Computing to Modern Tools

Nicolas began his narrative by recounting his early attempts to introduce Thomas to the world of programming, an endeavor that initially met with limited success. He humorously detailed how his efforts, ranging from teaching Scratch to developing Minecraft plugins in Java, didn't quite ignite the spark he had hoped for. The session then took a nostalgic turn, as Nicolas revisited the foundational experiences of his own youth, illustrating how he first encountered programming with vintage computers from the 1980s. This segment resonated with many in the audience, drawing parallels between the laborious loading times of cassette-based programs and the modern-day wait for PlayStation updates. This intergenerational bridge was pivotal, as it allowed Thomas to see the historical roots of computing. Ultimately, the breakthrough came not from structured lessons but through Thomas's organic engagement with tools and projects that naturally appealed to him, fostering a genuine, self-driven interest in the mechanics of code. This journey highlighted that the most effective learning often happens when curiosity leads the way.

## The Joy of Creation: Reinventing Code through Play

The heart of Thomas and Nicolas's presentation lay in the unexpected ways Thomas rediscovered the joy of coding. Far from being a passive recipient of instruction, Thomas embarked on his own creative ventures, transforming what might have been a chore into an exciting journey of discovery. He delved into the intricacies of game development, showcasing how even seemingly simple projects led to profound understanding of programming principles. The session also vividly illustrated Thomas's engagement with more advanced concepts, such as controlling robots with Arduino and bringing Lego Mindstorms creations to life through code. These hands-on projects allowed Thomas to reinvent and personalize his learning experience, making complex concepts tangible and enjoyable. The collaborative and playful environment fostered by Nicolas allowed Thomas to experiment, make mistakes, and learn organically, turning frustration into a catalyst for deeper learning. Their story served as a powerful reminder that true engagement with technology flourishes when individuals are empowered to explore, create, and find their own unique path within the vast landscape of digital innovation, emphasizing that the most impactful learning often happens outside traditional boundaries.

# Mobile Vision: Empowering Apps with Sight

At Devoxx France 2018, Christophe Jollivet, a technical agitator at Apside, presented a session titled *Des applications mobiles qui voient*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH5ICWzhTCk). Through live coding, he showcased Google’s Mobile Vision API, enabling Android and iOS apps to detect faces, read text, and scan barcodes offline. This session offers developers a practical guide to integrating vision capabilities into mobile apps.

## Face Detection and Landmarks

Jollivet began with a simple Android app capturing a photo, enhanced with Mobile Vision’s face detection. By adding dependencies to the project’s build file and declaring permissions in the manifest, he initialized a `FaceDetector` to identify facial landmarks (e.g., eyes, mouth) and draw rectangles around faces. Configurations like disabling classifications (e.g., smile detection) optimized performance for static images. The live demo displayed a photo with red rectangles and circles marking landmarks, demonstrating how to anonymize images or apply filters using facial coordinates. Despite the API’s limitations, such as partial head tilt detection, its offline functionality (downloading a 20MB native package once) ensures reliability in airplane mode.

## Text Recognition and Video Tracking

Expanding the demo, Jollivet implemented optical character recognition (OCR) using a `TextRecognizer`. The API detected text blocks, lines, and words, extracting content like “Devoxx France” from a background banner, though accuracy varied with font quality. For video, he used `CameraSource` and `GraphicOverlay` to track faces in real-time, overlaying a PNG mask on detected faces. The `MultiProcessor` and `Tracker` classes managed dynamic updates, resizing, and rotating the mask based on landmarks. While robust, the system struggled with extreme head angles, treating reappearing faces as new. These examples highlight Mobile Vision’s versatility for translation apps or invoice scanning.

# Sparking Creativity Through Coding

Saskia Blanc, a 12-year-old coding enthusiast, and her father Sébastien Blanc, a developer, delivered a session at Devoxx France 2018 titled *Le jaillissement de l'esprit*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p9y6FoLVi50). Through live coding, they traced the evolution of coding education from Logo to Scratch, inspiring parents to teach children programming. Their heartfelt presentation emphasized creativity and discovery.

## From Logo to Scratch

Sébastien shared his first coding memory at age eight, using BASIC on a Thomson MO5 to draw a yellow square, igniting his passion. He introduced Logo, created by Seymour Papert, which applied Piaget’s constructivism to let children learn through experimentation. In a live demo, Saskia coded a square using Logo’s turtle graphics, leveraging loops and procedures to draw variable-sized shapes. They transitioned to Scratch, Logo’s modern successor, where Saskia animated a cat sprite with walking costumes and a park backdrop. Scratch’s block-based interface and online community, supporting remixing akin to GitHub forking, make it accessible and collaborative for young coders.

## Groovy and Makey Makey Innovations

Saskia’s coding journey progressed to Groovy, a Java-like language. In a live demo, they modeled a `Cat` class inheriting from `Animal`, adding a `talk` method to print personalized messages. Saskia’s brother Loïs, aged nine, showcased a Scratch Super Mario remix, demonstrating rapid learning. The session concluded with a Makey Makey demo, using conductive objects to simulate keyboard inputs for a Scratch game, though technical issues arose. These examples underscore how coding fosters problem-solving and innovation, with resources available on [Saskia’s GitHub](https://github.com/saskia-blanc).

# Monitoring Microservices with JHipster Console

Pierre Besson, a full-stack developer and JHipster core team member, presented a session at Devoxx France 2018 titled *Monitoring en pratique d'une architecture microservice JHipster*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yG7zu0Nqa5Y). He demonstrated the JHipster Console, an open-source monitoring solution for microservices, using the ELK stack, Zipkin, and JHipster’s instrumentation. This session equips developers with tools to observe and debug distributed systems.

## Challenges of Microservice Monitoring

Microservices introduce complexity, with logs scattered across multiple instances and machines, making it hard to pinpoint issues, track call chains, or measure latency. Besson emphasized observability’s three pillars: logs, metrics, and traces. The JHipster Console centralizes these using Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana, with Zipkin for distributed tracing. In a demo, Besson generated a travel agency architecture with a gateway, booking, and catalog microservices using JHipster’s JDL. Docker Compose deployed the stack, including the Console, enabling log aggregation via Logback and trace collection via Spring Cloud Sleuth.

## Analyzing Logs, Metrics, and Traces

Using Kibana, Besson showcased dashboards filtering logs by microservice, instance, or error type, revealing a triggered bug in the booking service. Metrics dashboards displayed request rates (e.g., 3 calls/second on the gateway) and JVM stats (e.g., memory spikes to 1GB), aiding performance tuning. Zipkin traced call chains, identifying a 73ms latency in the booking API. Gatling simulations generated load, validating the Console’s ability to handle production-scale data. These tools simplify debugging and scaling, with pre-configured dashboards making monitoring accessible even for non-experts.

# Accelerate Your End-to-End Tests with Cypress (R. Bung)

In an engaging session at DevoxxFR2018, Rodolphe Bung, a seasoned developer from Expedia Group, introduced Cypress, a groundbreaking End-to-End (E2E) testing tool. He compellingly argued that Cypress offers a vastly superior developer experience compared to its long-standing predecessor, Selenium. Through a dynamic live-coding demonstration, Bung meticulously showcased Cypress's core functionalities and highlighted the key considerations that position it as a formidable solution in the modern web testing landscape.

## The Evolution of E2E Testing and Selenium's Challenges

Rodolphe Bung commenced his presentation by acknowledging Selenium's historical dominance in the realm of E2E testing, a tool that has been foundational since its inception in 2004, with the advent of WebDriver in 2007\. However, he swiftly pivoted to illustrate how the contemporary web environment, characterized by the proliferation of sophisticated frameworks like React and Angular, and the pervasive use of asynchronous operations and AJAX calls, has exposed inherent limitations in Selenium's architecture.

A primary challenge with Selenium, as articulated by Bung, lies in its reliance on remote communication. Tests execute outside the browser and interact with it through a separate process, often via a WebDriver. This architectural choice introduces latency, contributing to slower test execution times and making the debugging process considerably more arduous. When tests inevitably fail, Selenium frequently yields cryptic stack traces, which are notoriously difficult to interpret. Pinpointing the precise cause of an error—whether it stems from a failed AJAX request, an unrendered DOM element, or an elusive JavaScript bug—becomes a time-consuming and frustrating endeavor. Ultimately, the cumulative effect of these complexities, from intricate setup procedures to the opaque nature of debugging, often deters developers from actively engaging in E2E testing, thereby hindering comprehensive test coverage and delaying feedback loops.

## Cypress: A Developer-Centric Paradigm Shift

Cypress, conceived by Brian Mann in 2014 and launched into public beta in October 2017, distinguishes itself through a radical shift in approach, prioritizing the developer experience (DX) above all else. Its foundational innovation lies in executing tests directly within the browser, operating in the same run-loop as the application code itself. This architectural choice confers several profound advantages that fundamentally transform the E2E testing workflow.

The setup process for Cypress is remarkably straightforward, typically requiring no more than a simple `npm install cypress` command. The framework automatically generates a well-structured `cypress` directory containing intuitive folders for integrations, fixtures, plugins, support, and screenshots, streamlining test organization. Writing tests is made significantly easier due to its highly readable and concise syntax, allowing developers to express complex test scenarios with clarity.

One of Cypress's most compelling features is its unparalleled debugging capability. By running within the browser, Cypress gains direct and unfettered access to every facet of the application's execution: real-time DOM changes, comprehensive network requests (including all AJAX calls), and the dynamic application state. This level of insight, combined with Cypress’s remarkably clear error messages, allows developers to leverage familiar browser developer tools alongside Cypress’s dedicated test runner, transforming debugging from a painful ordeal into an efficient, almost intuitive process. Tests execute with remarkable speed, and Cypress natively supports parallel execution, which dramatically reduces the overall time required for large test suites. The intuitive user interface further enhances the experience, providing a visual overview of all tests, live command execution, and direct access to detailed browser insights, making E2E testing an integrated and enjoyable part of the development cycle.

# Chaos Engineering in Kubernetes with Operators

At Devoxx France 2018, Antoine Mazin and Etienne Coutaud, consultants at Cheops Technology, delivered a session titled *Ajouter du Chaos Engineering dans son cluster Kubernetes avec des opérateurs*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b8Ocmb0ComM). They introduced chaos engineering in Kubernetes, using a custom chaos-monkey operator to test application resilience by terminating pods, while exploring Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) and operators. This session demystifies these concepts for developers.

## Implementing Chaos with CRDs and Operators

The speakers began by explaining chaos engineering, inspired by Netflix’s Simian Army, which tests system resilience by inducing failures like latency or datacenter outages. In Kubernetes, they deployed a standard stack with deployments, replica sets, and services, then introduced a chaos operator pod in the `kube-system` namespace. This operator consumes `ChaosRule` CRDs, defining rules like “every minute, terminate a pod with label runtime=x.” CRDs extend Kubernetes with custom objects, allowing the operator to interpret rules and act, such as deleting pods. A live demo showed the operator synchronizing rules, logging events, and triggering pod terminations, with the replica set restoring the desired state, validating Kubernetes’ self-healing.

## Validating Resilience and Broader Use Cases

The chaos operator tests application resilience, ensuring compliance with the Twelve-Factor App principles, like ephemeral containers that tolerate restarts. It validates liveness and readiness probes: liveness probes restart unresponsive pods, while readiness probes remove unhealthy pods from load balancing. The demo highlighted graceful shutdowns within the termination grace period. Beyond chaos, CRDs and operators support diverse use cases. The Prometheus Operator simplifies monitoring by creating Prometheus instances via CRDs, collecting metrics from the chaos operator. Rook deploys Ceph storage clusters, while Ark manages backups. These examples show operators abstracting complexity, though the speakers cautioned about implementation challenges and portability, recommending Red Hat’s OpenShift blog for coding guidance.

# Mastering API Testing with Karate

Nicolas Comet and Benoît Prioux, developers at Lectra, presented a session at Devoxx France 2018 titled *Ceinture noire Karate en tests d’API REST*, available on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NYlPxd5dZOU). They showcased Karate, an open-source framework for testing REST APIs with a simple, Gherkin-inspired DSL, making it accessible to developers and QA teams. This session offers practical insights for integrating Karate into Java projects.

## Simplifying API Testing with Karate’s DSL

The speakers faced the challenge of testing an API gateway unifying microservices in a new web application. Traditional Java tests with HTTP libraries were verbose and hard to maintain, while tools like RestAssured still required coding. Karate’s plain-text DSL, built on Cucumber’s Gherkin syntax, allows scenarios like “Given path /movies, When method POST, Then status 201.” A live demo tested the Devoxx CFP API, verifying speaker details (e.g., company=Lectra) using a standalone Karate JAR, requiring only Java and Maven. The DSL’s readability enabled non-developers to write tests, with matchers validating JSON responses (e.g., ensuring an ID is non-null). Karate’s IDE integration and configuration file (karate-config.js) streamlined base URL management and environment switching.

## Advanced Features and Integration

Karate’s flexibility shone in a second demo, testing a Spring Boot API for movies and actors. Scenarios created films (e.g., “Karate Kid”), added actors (e.g., Jean-Claude Van Damme), and verified responses using variables to store IDs across requests. Karate supports parallel execution, JSON assertions, and data injection from external files or other Karate features, ensuring robust test suites. The framework integrates with Gatling for performance testing, supports Postman imports, and enables consumer-driven contract testing. The speakers highlighted Karate’s active community, with 500 GitHub stars, and comprehensive documentation by creator Peter Thomas, encouraging attendees to explore its versatility for microservice testing.
